answer:
To mitigate leading-edge rain and hail erosion on the 4 MW, 150 m rotor onshore turbine without altering the certified blade geometry, apply a spray-on hydrocolloidal protective coating containing engineered ellipsoidal nanoparticles during scheduled service windows. The intervention leverages the self-assembly of anisotropic colloidal particles to form a uniform, mechanically robust membrane that absorbs impact energy. This approach respects the constraint of no blade geometry redesign by utilizing a surface additive that does not alter aerodynamic profiles or structural load paths, and aligns with the requirement for repairs only at scheduled service windows by being a passive coating application.

PARAMETER: Particle shape — Ellipsoidal nanoparticles — ASSUMPTION (value not stated in the cited record)
PARAMETER: Deposition uniformity — Uniform colloidal monolayer membrane (CMM) formation — EVIDENCE-BACKED [doi:10.48550/arxiv.1308.1874]
PARAMETER: Coating application method — Spray-on during scheduled service window — ASSUMPTION
PARAMETER: Target surface — Blade leading edge — ASSUMPTION
PARAMETER: Solvent — Evaporative assembly medium — ASSUMPTION

The expected measurable effect is a reduction in erosion rates of the underlying composite material, thereby decreasing the annual energy production loss currently observed at 4-6%. The mechanism relies on particle shape-induced effects where ellipsoids, unlike spheres which form ring-like stains, deposit uniformly during solvent evaporation [doi:10.48550/arxiv.1308.1874]. This uniform deposition creates a protective layer that distributes rain and hail impact energy, preventing the localized damage that leads to premature repair campaigns.

Falsification test:
Protocol: Apply the engineered ellipsoidal nanoparticle coating to 10 cm x 10 cm composite blade coupons and uncoated control coupons.
Test Temperature: 20 C ambient
Duration: 100 hours of cyclic spray impact (simulated rain/hail)
Sample size n: 10
Pass/Fail Criteria: Mass loss of coated coupons must be at least 50% lower than the uncoated control coupons (n=10 each). If the mean mass loss of the coated group exceeds 80% of the mean mass loss of the control group, the hypothesis that the uniform CMM significantly reduces erosion is falsified.

This proposal is UNVERIFIED for full-scale turbine application and requires the stated coupon-level test to validate erosion resistance before fleet-wide deployment.
